  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Hallucination detection is critical for ensuring the reliability of large language models (LLMs) in context-based generation.
Prior work has explored intrinsic signals available during generation, among which attention offers a direct view of grounding behavior. However, existing approaches typically rely on coarse summaries that fail to capture fine-grained instabilities in attention.
Inspired by signal processing, we introduce a frequency-aware perspective on attention by analyzing its variation during generation.
We model attention distributions as discrete signals and extract high-frequency components that reflect rapid local changes in attention.
Our analysis reveals that hallucinated tokens are associated with high-frequency attention energy, reflecting fragmented and unstable grounding behavior.
Based on this insight, we develop a lightweight hallucination detector using high-frequency attention features.
Experiments on the RAGTruth and HalluRAG benchmarks show that our approach achieves performance gains over verification-based, internal-representation-based, and attention-based methods across models and tasks.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
        Code and data are available at <a href="https://github.com/siyaqi/FrequencyAwareHallucination" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/siyaqi/FrequencyAwareHallucination</a>.</span></span></span></p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center ltx_align_center"><span id="S0.F1.3.1" class="ltx_text"><img src="2602.18145v1/example.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:452/453;" width="452" height="453" alt="Refer to caption"></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Attention weights over context and previously generated tokens for a grounded token (blue, “rainy”) and a hallucinated token (red, “December”) in a context-based QA example.
</span></figcaption>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across many natural language processing tasks, yet they can produce <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">hallucinated outputs</em> that are fluent but not supported by the given input or external facts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">van Deemter, 2024</a>)</cite>. This issue is especially pronounced in the <span id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">context-based generation</span> settings,
such as the summarization task, where models are explicitly expected to ground in a provided source context <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>.
Therefore, effective hallucination detection is essential for building trustworthy language systems and enabling downstream mitigation strategies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A common approach to hallucination detection verifies model outputs against the source context, for example, using semantic similarity measures or LLM-as-a-judge frameworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kryscinski et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Laban et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Manakul et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Such methods compare the output with contextual evidence and are applied post hoc, rather than reflecting the model’s generation dynamics.
Motivated by this limitation, recent work has explored hallucination detection from intrinsic signals available during generation, including token probabilities, hidden representations, and attention patterns
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chuang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>. Among these signals, attention is particularly informative, as it directly reflects how the model allocates content focus during generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wiegreffe and Pinter, 2019</a>)</cite>.
Prior studies have shown that hallucinated generations are often associated with unstable or diffuse attention behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sriramanan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. However, <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">how to quantify attention stability or uncertainty remains an open problem</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Most existing attention-based methods summarize attention using coarse statistics, such as attention mass, entropy, or transition patterns <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chuang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>. While effective at capturing overall concentration, such scaling-based metrics often discard fine-grained sequential variation.
For example, in Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we prompt LLaMA-2-7B-Chat with a context-based question and require the model to answer strictly using the provided context. Although most generated tokens align well with the source, the model produces a hallucinated token containing month names (e.g., “December”) that does not appear in the context.
Compared to a grounded token, the attention distribution associated with this hallucinated token exhibits noticeably stronger local fluctuations across context positions, with sharper peaks and more abrupt changes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, we argue that directly mapping an attention sequence to a single scalar cannot fully capture the structure of attention patterns. Inspired by signal processing, we treat attention weights over context tokens as a discrete temporal signal indexed by token position, where stable grounding corresponds to smooth, slowly varying signals, while instability manifests as rapid local oscillations.
To explicitly quantify such variation, we perform frequency-aware decomposition of the attention signal: low-frequency components capture global trends of attention allocation across the context, whereas high-frequency components isolate sharp spikes and abrupt local changes. We hypothesize that hallucinated tokens are associated with energy in these high-frequency attention components.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by this perspective, we study contextual hallucination detection via frequency-aware analysis of attention signals. Our contributions are threefold:
<span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1)</span> We formulate attention as discrete signals and introduce a unified frequency-based framework for analyzing attention variation for hallucination detection.
<span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2)</span> We instantiate this framework using simple yet efficient high-frequency extraction operators, enabling the quantification of attention instability at both token and span levels.
<span id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(3)</span> Through extensive experiments across multiple models and tasks, we show that frequency-based attention features can improve hallucination detection over existing verification-based, internal representation-based, and attention-based baselines.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S1.F2.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center ltx_align_center"><span id="S1.F2.3.1" class="ltx_text"><img src="2602.18145v1/hypothese_compare.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:452/380;" width="452" height="380" alt="Refer to caption"></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Three hypotheses for identifying hallucination tokens from incoming attention patterns.
We illustrate three representative assumptions for distinguishing well-grounded tokens (✓) from potential hallucinations (✗) based on the incoming attention to the next generated token.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we review attention weight as an intrinsic signal for hallucination and introduce a frequency-based perspective that characterizes attention instability beyond the coarse allocation statistics.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Attention-based Hallucination Detection</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each generated token, the attention distribution reflects how the model aggregates information from the source context and previously generated tokens, and is therefore widely used as an intrinsic signal of grounding and information usage <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Campbell et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Snyder et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Prior work exploits attention for hallucination detection by making different assumptions about grounded generation behavior.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">One line of work focuses on attention transitions, using backward attention from generated tokens to the source context as an indicator of grounding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chuang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ogasa and Arase, 2025</a>)</cite>. Another line analyzes the distributional properties of attention, either by identifying context tokens emphasized by specific attention heads <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>)</cite> or by summarizing attention uncertainty using entropy-based measures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vazhentsev et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. These approaches are motivated by the intuition that grounded generation exhibits focused and consistent evidence attribution, whereas hallucination is associated with diffuse or ambiguous attention.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As illustrated in <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 2</span></a>, existing attention-based methods primarily capture <em id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">where</em> attention is allocated or <em id="S2.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how</em> dispersed it is, but do not explicitly model the internal structure of attention patterns. In contrast, our hypothesis emphasizes the <em id="S2.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">coherence</em> of attention distributions, motivated by the observation that hallucinated generations often exhibit fragmented or rapidly oscillating attention behavior that is not captured by static allocation or entropy-based statistics.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S2.F3.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.F3.3.1" class="ltx_text"><img src="2602.18145v1/main.png" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:880/334;" width="880" height="334" alt="Refer to caption"></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S2.F3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Overview of frequency-aware attention modeling for hallucination detection.
Attention weights are extracted from each layer and head (<math id="S2.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> layers and <math id="S2.F3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> heads in total), treated as token-level signals, and decomposed using high-pass filtering to isolate high-frequency variations (<math id="S2.F3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\text{high}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mtext>high</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\text{high}}</annotation></semantics></math>), whose energy is aggregated for hallucination detection.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>A Frequency-based View of Attention</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To capture attention variation beyond static summaries, we model attention weights over tokens as discrete signals.
In signal processing, smooth and coherent patterns are naturally represented by low-frequency components, whereas abrupt changes and local irregularities manifest as high-frequency components. As such, frequency analysis offers a natural characterization of attention stability and instability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Rather than committing to a single formulation, we consider several standard operators that instantiate this frequency-based view with complementary inductive biases.
The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cooley et al., 1969</a>)</cite> provides a global decomposition of attention signals into frequency components.
The Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mallat, 1989</a>)</cite> uses localized basis functions, allowing abrupt attention changes to be captured while preserving positional information.
As a simpler local alternative, the discrete Laplacian operator <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oppenheim and Schafer, 1997</a>)</cite> directly highlights second-order differences directly in the token domain, acting as an implicit high-pass filter.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Despite their different forms, these operators share a common goal: isolating high-frequency variation that reflects fragmented or rapidly oscillating attention behavior. Together, they provide a unified frequency-based framework for analyzing attention instability during generation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Frequency-Aware Attention Modeling</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Viewing attention from a frequency-aware perspective offers a principled way to analyze variation patterns that are difficult to characterize directly in the token domain.
In this framework (shown in <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.1 Attention-based Hallucination Detection ‣ 2 Background ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 3</span></a>), attention weights over tokens are modeled as discrete signals, enabling the use of frequency-aware operators to quantify how attention evolves and fluctuates during generation, beyond what is captured by aggregate statistics.
We first demonstrate our motivation and intuition through a simplified setting here.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Motivation and Intuition</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While a rigorous mechanistic understanding of attention behavior under hallucinated generation remains an open problem, we can gain preliminary insights from a simplified toy setting. Specifically, consider a scenario where tokens come from several latent semantic sources. As the number of such sources increases, neighboring tokens are more likely to differ in topic, causing the compatibility between the current token and its context to change abruptly across adjacent positions. Such abrupt local changes translate into adjacent differences in attention weights, yielding jagged attention patterns along the sequence (see <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A A three-step proof that larger 𝐾 increases (a lower bound on) attention roughness ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix A</span></a> for a complete proof). Although such toy analysis relies on simplifying assumptions, it formalizes a general link between semantic heterogeneity and attention instability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Real LLM attention is, however, substantially far more complex. It is shaped by architectural depth, multi-head specialization, and long-range contextual interactions, all of which can give rise to higher-order and multi-scale instabilities that cannot be captured by adjacent difference measures alone.
From a signal-processing perspective, adjacent differences correspond only to a primitive form of high-pass filtering. Frequency-aware operators (e.g., DFT, DWT, Laplacian), by contrast, are able to systematically extract high-frequency components across multiple resolutions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Donoho and Johnstone, 1998</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stein and Shakarchi, 2011</a>)</cite>. This motivates our frequency-aware framework for quantifying complex attention instabilities associated with hallucination detection.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Problem Setup</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider a context-based generation setting, where a language model generates a response <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{gen}=(gen_{1},\dots,gen_{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐠𝐞𝐧</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{gen}=(gen_{1},\dots,gen_{T})</annotation></semantics></math> conditioned on a retrieved context <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{ctx}=(ctx_{1},\dots,ctx_{N})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐜𝐭𝐱</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{ctx}=(ctx_{1},\dots,ctx_{N})</annotation></semantics></math>.
At each generation step <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, the model produces token <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> based on <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{ctx},\mathbf{gen}_{&lt;i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐜𝐭𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐠𝐞𝐧</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{ctx},\mathbf{gen}_{&lt;i})</annotation></semantics></math> and exposes attention weights across layers and heads.
Our primary task is token-level hallucination detection: for each generated token <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, predict whether <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is supported by the provided context.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Rather than operating on attention weights directly, our detector uses frequency-aware features derived from attention.
For each step <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> when generating <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, we compute a feature vector <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}</annotation></semantics></math> (defined in §<a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Energy-Based High-Frequency Instability ‣ 3 Frequency-Aware Attention Modeling ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>) and predict</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{r}_{i}=f(\mathbf{v})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐯</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{r}_{i}=f(\mathbf{v}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is a lightweight linear classifier, and <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{r}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{r}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> indicates a prediction result for hallucination or non-hallucination.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Attention as Discrete Signals</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At generation step <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, we extract attention weight distributions from all transformer layers and heads.
We distinguish two types of attention signals: <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">context-directed attention</em>, attending from the current token <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> to the input context tokens, and <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">generated-token attention</em>, attending to previously generated tokens before this generation step.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each layer <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l\in\{1,\dots,L\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l\in\{1,\dots,L\}</annotation></semantics></math> and head <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h\in\{1,\dots,H\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h\in\{1,\dots,H\}</annotation></semantics></math>, we define the context-directed attention vector and the generated-token attention vector:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E2X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=[a^{(ctx)}_{l,h,1},a^{(ctx)}_{l,h,2},\dots,a^{(ctx)}_{l,h,N}]\in\mathbb{R}^{N}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=[a^{(ctx)}_{l,h,1},a^{(ctx)}_{l,h,2},\dots,a^{(ctx)}_{l,h,N}]\in\mathbb{R}^{N},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E2Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle a^{(gen)}_{l,h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle a^{(gen)}_{l,h}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=[a^{(gen)}_{l,h,1},a^{(gen)}_{l,h,2},\dots,a^{(gen)}_{l,h,i-1}]\in\mathbb{R}^{i-1}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=[a^{(gen)}_{l,h,1},a^{(gen)}_{l,h,2},\dots,a^{(gen)}_{l,h,i-1}]\in\mathbb{R}^{i-1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">which respectively capture attention over <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> context tokens and the previously generated tokens before <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Both <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{(ctx)}_{l,h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{(ctx)}_{l,h}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{(gen)}_{l,h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{(gen)}_{l,h}</annotation></semantics></math> are treated as one-dimensional discrete signals that indexed by token position.
Taking the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) as an example, and let <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denote DFT.
Mapping the attention weight vector to the frequency domain yields</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{a}_{l,h}^{(\tau)}=\mathcal{F}\big(a^{(\tau)}_{l,h}\big)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{a}_{l,h}^{(\tau)}=\mathcal{F}\big(a^{(\tau)}_{l,h}\big),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\in\{ctx,gen\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\in\{ctx,gen\}</annotation></semantics></math>; details for the DWT and Laplacian operators are provided in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Frequency-aware Operators’ Energy Equivalence ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Energy-Based High-Frequency Instability</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Building on the frequency-based view, we isolate and quantify high-frequency components of attention weight signals.
The formulation applies uniformly to both context-directed and previously generated-token attention.
To simplify notation, we use <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math> to denote the attention signal obtained for <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>,
corresponding to either <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{(ctx)}_{l,h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{(ctx)}_{l,h}</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{(gen)}_{l,h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{(gen)}_{l,h}</annotation></semantics></math> for layer <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> and head <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>,
with signal length <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given an attention signal <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math>, we extract high-frequency component by high-pass operator (e.g., DFT, DWT, Laplacian)</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{hf}}=\mathcal{F}_{\text{high}}(\mathbf{x})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>hf</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mtext>high</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{hf}}=\mathcal{F}_{\text{high}}(\mathbf{x}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\text{high}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mtext>high</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\text{high}}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes a high-pass operator that suppresses smooth, low-frequency components while preserving high-frequency components representing rapid local variation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For transform-based operators such as DFT and DWT, <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\text{high}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mtext>high</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\text{high}}</annotation></semantics></math> is implemented by frequency-domain masking followed by an inverse transform.
Let <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})</annotation></semantics></math> denote the DFT coefficients.
We retain only high-frequency components by applying a frequency mask by following definition:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathrm{hf}}_{k}=\begin{cases}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k},&amp;k\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{high}},\\
0,&amp;\text{otherwise},\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi><mi>hf</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><mi>high</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext>otherwise</mtext><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathrm{hf}}_{k}=\begin{cases}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k},&amp;k\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{high}},\\
0,&amp;\text{otherwise},\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{high}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒦</mi><mi>high</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{high}}</annotation></semantics></math> indexes the retained high-frequency band.
The corresponding high-frequency component <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{hf}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>hf</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{hf}}</annotation></semantics></math> in the temporal domain is obtained via inverse transform.
Wavelet- and Laplacian-based operators provide alternative realizations of <math id="S3.SS4.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\text{high}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mtext>high</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\text{high}}</annotation></semantics></math> that emphasize localized high-frequency variation, while serving the same purpose of isolating rapid attention fluctuations (detailed in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Frequency-aware Operators’ Energy Equivalence ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We summarize the magnitude of high-frequency variation by using the <math id="S3.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm on the high-frequency component</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\|\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{hf}}\|_{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>hf</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\|\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{hf}}\|_{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p4.2" class="ltx_p">which measures the energy of high-frequency components in the attention signal in temporal domain.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The use of the <math id="S3.SS4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm is theoretically motivated by <span id="S3.SS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Parseval’s theorem</span>, which establishes the equivalence between signal energy measured in the temporal domain and that measured in the frequency domain.
For DFT-based filtering,</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{hf}}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}|\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{hf}}_{j}|^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathrm{hf}}_{k}|^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>hf</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>hf</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi><mi>hf</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{hf}}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}|\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{hf}}_{j}|^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathrm{hf}}_{k}|^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>

<p id="S3.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Applying the above procedure independently to each attention head and each attention type yields a score <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho^{(\tau)}_{l,h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho^{(\tau)}_{l,h}</annotation></semantics></math> for every layer <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>, head <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>, and attention type <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\in\{ctx,gen\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\in\{ctx,gen\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p6.2" class="ltx_p">We aggregate these scores across all layers and heads to form feature vectors <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}^{(ctx)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}^{(ctx)}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}^{(gen)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}^{(gen)}</annotation></semantics></math> for context-directed and generated-token attention, respectively. We then concatenate these vectors as <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}</annotation></semantics></math> and feed them into the classifier to obtain the final prediction <math id="S3.SS4.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{r}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{r}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> for token-level hallucination detection.
As a robustness check under coarser supervision, we also report span-level results by applying a fixed sliding window, averaging the feature vectors within each window, and feeding the averaged vectors into the classifier.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiment Setting</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Baselines</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this study, we evaluate our approach against a diverse set of representative baselines for comparison, spanning verification-based, internal representation-based, and attention-based paradigms, as detailed below.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Verification-based Methods.</span> <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SelfCheckGPT</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Manakul et al., 2023</a>)</cite> detects hallucinations by measuring stochastic consistency across multiple responses sampled from a language model.
<span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RefChecker</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> extracts claims from model outputs and verifies them against context using a dedicated checker.
Both of them operate in a prompt-based manner and rely on the generative behavior of the underlying LLM.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Internal Representation-Based Methods.</span> <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EigenScore</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite> leverages output probability distributions to construct a semantic consistency graph and quantifies uncertainty via spectral analysis.
<span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ReDeEP</span> integrates internal signals from hidden states and attention mass to detect hallucinations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Both methods represent strong internal-signal-based baselines.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attention-based Methods.</span> We include <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lookback-Lens</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chuang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> as a strong attention-based baseline, which characterizes hallucination by quantifying the allocation of attention between retrieved context tokens and previously generated tokens.
In addition, we implement two mechanistic attention-based baselines based on attention <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">variance</span> and attention <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">entropy</span>.
For these baselines, statistics are computed separately over context tokens and generated tokens, and concatenated across all attention heads to form a unified feature representation for classification.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Implementation Settings</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the effectiveness and robustness of our method, we conduct experiments across three widely used open-source LLMs, including LLaMA-7B-Chat, LLaMA-13B-Chat, and Mistral-7B-Instruct, covering diverse model sizes and architectures.
Experiments are conducted on two context-based hallucination benchmarks: RAGTruth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, covering question answering (QA), data-to-text (D2T), and summarization (Summ), and HalluRAG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ridder and Schilling, 2024</a>)</cite>, which focuses on the QA task.
Both datasets provide token-level hallucination annotations.
Frequency-aware attention features are aggregated using a single-layer logistic regression classifier, and detection is performed at either the token or span level.
We report F1 and AUROC on the test sets, using AUROC as the primary metric.
Additional details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS3" title="C.3 Model Details ‣ Appendix C Experiment Details ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Results and Analysis</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Overall Performance</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Across all evaluated models and datasets, frequency-aware analysis of attention consistently improves hallucination detection over verification-based, internal representation-based, and attention-based baselines.
Explicitly isolating high-frequency components of attention yields stronger performance than aggregate statistics such as variance or entropy, highlighting the importance of modeling fine-grained attention variation.
By focusing on <em id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how</em> attention varies within the sequence rather than <em id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">where</em> attention mass is allocated, frequency-aware features provide complementary discriminative signals beyond attention mass alone.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These improvements hold across diverse task formats and models.
For example, on summarization task, Fourier-high improves AUROC by 6.6% over Lookback-Lens on LLaMA-13B, and by 2.7% on LLaMA-7B.
This consistency across datasets and generation settings suggests that high-frequency attention variation captures a general property of ungrounded generation, rather than task- or structure-specific artifacts.
We further evaluate cross-domain generalization by training the detector on one task and testing it on another (see <a href="#A4.T2" title="Table A2 ‣ D.1 Cross-domain Transfer Analysis ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table A2</span></a>).
Compared to Lookback-Lens, our method exhibits substantially more robust transfer performance, indicating that frequency-aware attention features generalize better across task boundaries.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Among all three operators, Fourier-based features achieve the strongest overall performance, followed by wavelets and the Laplacian.
This ordering aligns with both their inductive biases and the structural properties of attention signals: attention distributions are typically sparse and highly uneven across positions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nawrot et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, often dominated by a small subset of tokens, which favors operators that aggregate high-frequency variation globally.
Correspondingly, Fourier-based filtering is particularly effective at capturing global high-frequency energy, while wavelets and the Laplacian emphasize progressively more localized variation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">

<td id="S5.T2.11.1.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="S5.T2.11.1.10.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fourier-high</span></td>
<td id="S5.T2.11.1.10.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S5.T2.11.1.10.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">0.7063</span></td>
<td id="S5.T2.11.1.10.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center"><span id="S5.T2.11.1.10.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">0.8585</span></td>

</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Span-level Hallucination Detection</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In practical settings, hallucinations often occur as contiguous spans rather than isolated tokens.
To evaluate whether our method generalizes beyond token-level detection, we conduct span-level hallucination detection under a sliding-window setting, where consecutive tokens are grouped into fixed-size chunks and classified at the chunk level.
Following prior work such as Lookback-Lens, we use a chunk size of 8 and aggregate attention features within each chunk to form a single representation for prediction.
Results across the two benchmarks are reported in <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.1 Overall Performance ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 2</span></a>, with full per-task results provided in <a href="#A4.T3" title="Table A3 ‣ D.2 Full Results of Span-level Detection ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table A3</span></a> for RagTruth.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Span-level evaluation is more challenging due to coarser supervision and the need to aggregate signals across multiple tokens. Despite this increased difficulty, Fourier- and Wavelet-based variants achieve the strongest performance on all three tasks.
Fourier-based features yield consistent gains over Lookback-Lens, improving AUROC by 5.3% on LLaMA-7B (RAGTruth-Avg), with a particularly improvement of 10.1% on the summarization task (see <a href="#A4.T3" title="Table A3 ‣ D.2 Full Results of Span-level Detection ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table A3</span></a>).
Overall, these results indicate that frequency-based features remain robust when individual token-level signals are aggregated into spans, and that our approach generalizes naturally from token- to span-level hallucination detection across multiple tasks without requiring architectural modification.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S5.F4.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center ltx_align_center"><span id="S5.F4.3.1" class="ltx_text"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18145v1/avg_auroc_highvlow_with_full.svg" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/282;" width="429" height="282"></object></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.F4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> Comparing full-, low-, and high-pass Fourier attention features. Average AUROC across models under token- and span-level evaluation settings.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Ablation Study on High/Low-pass Components</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further analyze the contribution of different frequency bands by comparing low-pass, high-pass, and full-spectrum attention features, as shown in <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Span-level Hallucination Detection ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 4</span></a>.
Across all models and both token- and span-level evaluation settings, high-pass components achieve the strongest performance, while low-pass and full-spectrum features perform comparably.
This pattern suggests that, without explicitly isolating high-frequency variation, attention signals are largely dominated by low-frequency components that offer limited discriminative power for hallucination detection.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Low-frequency components mainly reflect smooth, global alignment patterns common to both grounded and hallucinated outputs, whereas high-pass components emphasize rapid local irregularities in attention that are more closely associated with unstable generation behavior.
Additional analyses on Fourier frequency cutoffs and Wavelet detail levels are provided in <a href="#A4.F1" title="Figure A1 ‣ D.2 Full Results of Span-level Detection ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure A1</span></a>, <a href="#A4.T4" title="Table A4 ‣ D.2 Full Results of Span-level Detection ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table A4</span></a>, and <a href="#A4.T5" title="Table A5 ‣ D.2 Full Results of Span-level Detection ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table A5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Understanding Frequency-Aware Features</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To better understand how frequency-aware attention features contribute to hallucination detection, we analyze the learned linear classifier from three perspectives: layer-level importance, head-level sparsity, and the relative contribution of context versus generated attention.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.4.1 </span>Layer-wise Importance</h4>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 5.4.1 Layer-wise Importance ‣ 5.4 Understanding Frequency-Aware Features ‣ 5 Results and Analysis ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 5</span></a>, we report the average absolute classifier coefficients assigned to attention heads in each layer. The importance of high-frequency attention signals is clearly non-uniform across model depth.
For Fourier-based features, importance peaks in the middle layers, with a pronounced maximum around layer 14. These layers are commonly associated with higher-level semantic processing and factual reasoning, suggesting that hallucination-related attention instability emerges most prominently once the model gradually transitions from surface-level decoding to semantic composition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chuang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S5.F5.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center ltx_align_center"><span id="S5.F5.3.1" class="ltx_text"><img src="2602.18145v1/layerwise_fourier_llama_2_7b_chat.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/319;" width="429" height="319" alt="Refer to caption"></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S5.F5.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Layer-wise importance of high-frequency Fourier-high attention features for LLaMA-7B.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Across almost all layers, span-level (dashed line) assigns higher importance weights than token-level detection (solid line). This indicates that aggregating attention signals over longer spans amplifies structured high-frequency variation, rather than weakening it, further supporting the robustness of frequency-aware features under coarser supervision.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">5.4.2 </span>Head-wise Sparsity</h4>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond layer-level trends, we examine whether detection signals are broadly distributed across heads or concentrated in a small subset. To this end, we perform detection using only the Top-<math id="S5.SS4.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> attention heads ranked by their average absolute classifier coefficients.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S5.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">AUROC Results for LLaMA-7B: Original vs. Top-<math id="S5.T3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> head only performance.</span></figcaption>

<td id="S5.T3.5.8.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;" rowspan="2"><span id="S5.T3.5.8.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Original</span></td>
<td id="S5.T3.5.8.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;" colspan="3"><span id="S5.T3.5.8.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Top-<math id="S5.T3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> heads</span></td></tr>
