<section id="A1.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.6 </span>Summary of the logical connection between Sub-claims 1–3</h3>

<section id="A1.SS6.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">How the pieces fit together.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The proof decomposes the <math id="A1.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-dependence into three steps:</p>
<ol id="A1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A1.I1.i1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(i)</span></span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Sub-claim 1)</span> Increasing <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> increases the probability that adjacent inputs come from different mixture components:
<math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pr(c_{j+1}\neq c_{j})=1-\frac{1}{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>Pr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>≠</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>K</mi></mfrac></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pr(c_{j+1}\neq c_{j})=1-\frac{1}{K}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A1.I1.i2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(ii)</span></span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Sub-claim 2)</span> Under separability along the attention score direction <math id="A1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math>, a component switch forces a nontrivial expected squared jump in adjacent logits, yielding a lower bound
<math id="A1.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}[(s_{t,j+1}-s_{t,j})^{2}]\geq(1-\frac{1}{K})\Delta^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>K</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}[(s_{t,j+1}-s_{t,j})^{2}]\geq(1-\frac{1}{K})\Delta^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (up to additional noise energy).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A1.I1.i3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(iii)</span></span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Sub-claim 3)</span> A pairwise identity for softmax shows
<math id="A1.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{t,j+1}-\alpha_{t,j}=m\tanh(\Delta s/2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>tanh</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{t,j+1}-\alpha_{t,j}=m\tanh(\Delta s/2)</annotation></semantics></math>, and under non-degeneracy (<math id="A1.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> not vanishing too often) this yields
<math id="A1.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{t,j+1}-\alpha_{t,j})^{2}]\gtrsim\mathbb{E}[(\Delta s)^{2}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≳</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{t,j+1}-\alpha_{t,j})^{2}]\gtrsim\mathbb{E}[(\Delta s)^{2}]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="A1.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Chaining (i)–(iii) and summing over <math id="A1.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> proves Theorem <a href="#A1.Thmtheorem9" title="Theorem A.9 (Monotone 𝐾-dependent lower bound for attention roughness). ‣ A.5 Main theorem and concise proof via Sub-claims 1–3 ‣ Appendix A A three-step proof that larger 𝐾 increases (a lower bound on) attention roughness ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.9</span></a>, which provides a monotone increasing-in-<math id="A1.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> lower bound on <math id="A1.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}[R_{t}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}[R_{t}]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Frequency-aware Operators’ Energy Equivalence</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this appendix section, we provide additional technical details on the spectral operators used in our framework and clarify how high-frequency energy can be consistently quantified using the <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm.
We show that the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), and the discrete Laplacian operator all provide principled ways to extract high-frequency components from discrete attention signals, and that their corresponding <math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norms measure comparable notions of signal energy despite operating in different domains.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Discrete Fourier Transform</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We begin with the DFT, which provides a global frequency-domain representation of discrete signals.
Given a token-level attention signal <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{l,h}\in\mathbb{R}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{l,h}\in\mathbb{R}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> from layer <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> and head <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>, its DFT is defined as</p>
<table id="A2.E13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E13.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{a}_{l,h}(\omega)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}a_{l,h}(t)\,e^{-i2\pi\omega t/T},\quad\omega=0,\dots,T-1." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo rspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>ω</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msup><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{a}_{l,h}(\omega)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}a_{l,h}(t)\,e^{-i2\pi\omega t/T},\quad\omega=0,\dots,T-1.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(13)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A frequency-domain high-pass filter <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M(\omega)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M(\omega)</annotation></semantics></math> can be applied to isolate high-frequency components, yielding</p>
<table id="A2.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{z}^{\mathrm{hf}}_{l,h}(\omega)=M(\omega)\,\hat{a}_{l,h}(\omega)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mi>hf</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{z}^{\mathrm{hf}}_{l,h}(\omega)=M(\omega)\,\hat{a}_{l,h}(\omega),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(14)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M(\omega)=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M(\omega)=1</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega\in\Omega_{\text{high}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ω</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mtext>high</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega\in\Omega_{\text{high}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> otherwise.
The corresponding high-frequency signal in the token domain is obtained via the inverse DFT.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The use of the <math id="A2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm as a hallucination score is justified by the <em id="A2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Parseval’s theorem</em> in Section <a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Energy-Based High-Frequency Instability ‣ 3 Frequency-Aware Attention Modeling ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>, which guarantees energy equivalence between the token and frequency domains:</p>
<table id="A2.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|z^{\mathrm{hf}}_{l,h}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_{\text{high}}}\left|\hat{a}_{l,h}(\omega)\right|^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mi>hf</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>T</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>ω</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mtext>high</mtext></msub></mrow></munder><msup><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|z^{\mathrm{hf}}_{l,h}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{\omega\in\Omega_{\text{high}}}\left|\hat{a}_{l,h}(\omega)\right|^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Thus, the score <math id="A2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{l,h}=\|z^{\mathrm{hf}}_{l,h}\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mi>hf</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{l,h}=\|z^{\mathrm{hf}}_{l,h}\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> directly measures the total high-frequency energy of the attention signal, capturing rapid oscillations and global irregularities across the token sequence.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Discrete Wavelet Transform</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">DWT provides a multi-resolution analysis of discrete signals, decomposing an attention signal into components at different spatial scales.
Using an orthonormal wavelet basis (e.g., Daubechies wavelets), the attention signal <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{l,h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{l,h}</annotation></semantics></math> is decomposed into approximation coefficients <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c_{A}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>𝐀</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c_{A}}</annotation></semantics></math> and detail coefficients <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c_{D}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>𝐃</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c_{D}}</annotation></semantics></math> at multiple scales.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In our framework, the high-frequency component <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z^{\mathrm{hf}}_{l,h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mi>hf</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^{\mathrm{hf}}_{l,h}</annotation></semantics></math> is reconstructed from <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c_{D}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>𝐃</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c_{D}}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponding to fine scales, which capture localized and abrupt changes in attention.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">By <em id="A2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Parseval’s theorem</em>, the energy of the attention signal is preserved under an orthonormal wavelet transform, and equals the sum of squared wavelet coefficients.
Let <math id="A2.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{j,k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{j,k}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the detail coefficient <math id="A2.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c_{D}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>𝐃</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c_{D}}</annotation></semantics></math> at scale <math id="A2.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> and position <math id="A2.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>. Then,</p>
<table id="A2.E16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|z^{\mathrm{hf}}_{l,h}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{\text{high}}}\sum_{k}|d_{j,k}|^{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mi>hf</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒥</mi><mtext>high</mtext></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mi>k</mi></munder><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|z^{\mathrm{hf}}_{l,h}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{\text{high}}}\sum_{k}|d_{j,k}|^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{J}_{\text{high}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒥</mi><mtext>high</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{J}_{\text{high}}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the set of high-frequency scales.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Accordingly, the score <math id="A2.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{l,h}=\|z^{\mathrm{hf}}_{l,h}\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mi>hf</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{l,h}=\|z^{\mathrm{hf}}_{l,h}\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> quantifies the localized detail energy of the attention distribution, emphasizing sharp transitions and spatially concentrated irregularities that are characteristic of unstable attention patterns.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Discrete Laplacian Operator</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The discrete Laplacian operator provides a spatial-domain alternative for extracting high-frequency variation.
For a one-dimensional attention signal <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{l,h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{l,h}</annotation></semantics></math>, the discrete Laplacian <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐋</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{L}</annotation></semantics></math> computes second-order differences, measuring how much each token’s attention deviates from the average of its immediate neighbors.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The <math id="A2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm of the Laplacian response,</p>
<table id="A2.E17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\mathbf{L}a_{l,h}\|_{2}^{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝐋</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\mathbf{L}a_{l,h}\|_{2}^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(17)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">corresponds to the discrete <em id="A2.SS3.p2.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Dirichlet energy</em> of the signal, which quantifies its roughness or lack of smoothness <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sandryhaila and Moura, 2014</a>)</cite>.
A higher energy value indicates that the attention distribution exhibits rapid local oscillations or fragmentation, rather than smooth decay or coherent concentration.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The role of the Laplacian as a high-frequency operator can be further understood through its frequency response.
In the spectral domain, the discrete Laplacian corresponds to a filter with transfer function</p>
<table id="A2.E18" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H(\omega)=2-2\cos(\omega)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(\omega)=2-2\cos(\omega).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(18)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">As <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H(\omega)\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(\omega)\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>, suppressing low-frequency (smooth) components.
As <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega\to\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega\to\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H(\omega)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(\omega)</annotation></semantics></math> attains its maximum value, strongly amplifying high-frequency components associated with abrupt transitions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Consequently, the score <math id="A2.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{l,h}=\|\mathbf{L}a_{l,h}\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝐋</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{l,h}=\|\mathbf{L}a_{l,h}\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> serves as a computationally efficient proxy for high-frequency energy, capturing localized attention instability without requiring an explicit frequency-domain transform.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Experiment Details</h2>

<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Implementation of Baselines</h3>

<section id="A3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">C.1.1 </span>Verification and Probabilistic Baselines</h4>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For verification-based baselines, both <span id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SelfCheckGPT</span> and <span id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RefChecker</span> use <span id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o-mini</span> as the backbone model for claim extraction and factual verification.
For probabilistic consistency baselines, <span id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EigenScore</span> constructs a similarity matrix <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐒</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{S}</annotation></semantics></math> based on BERTScore between generated responses, and derives a consistency score from the largest eigenvalue <math id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{S})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐒</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{S})</annotation></semantics></math>.
<span id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ReDeEP</span> computes two complementary signals during generation: an external context score derived from attention allocation over input tokens, and a parametric knowledge score derived from feed-forward network activations, following the original implementation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Both EigenScore and ReDeEP are strong unsupervised methods specifically designed for hallucination detection that leverage internal model signals, including attention. Despite not being directly trained for the task, they have shown powerful performance and are therefore included as competitive and fair baselines in our comparison.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">C.1.2 </span>Attention-based Feature Extraction</h4>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For all intrinsic, attention-based methods (including entropy-based baselines and our frequency-aware features), we extract attention weights from all transformer layers and heads.
Let <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}=\{\mathbf{A}_{l,h}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}=\{\mathbf{A}_{l,h}\}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the collection of attention distributions, where <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}_{l,h}\in\mathbb{R}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}_{l,h}\in\mathbb{R}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> is the token-level attention vector from layer <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> and head <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chuang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, we partition attention into context-directed attention <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}^{(c)}_{l,h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}^{(c)}_{l,h}</annotation></semantics></math> and generated-token attention <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}^{(g)}_{l,h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}^{(g)}_{l,h}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For a given head, a feature extraction function <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is applied to the corresponding attention distribution.
Aggregating across all layers and heads yields separate feature vectors for context and generated attention:</p>
<table id="A3.E19" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}^{(c)}=[f(\mathbf{A}^{(c)}_{1,1}),\dots,f(\mathbf{A}^{(c)}_{L,H})]^{\top},\quad\mathbf{v}^{(g)}=[f(\mathbf{A}^{(g)}_{1,1}),\dots,f(\mathbf{A}^{(g)}_{L,H})]^{\top}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}^{(c)}=[f(\mathbf{A}^{(c)}_{1,1}),\dots,f(\mathbf{A}^{(c)}_{L,H})]^{\top},\quad\mathbf{v}^{(g)}=[f(\mathbf{A}^{(g)}_{1,1}),\dots,f(\mathbf{A}^{(g)}_{L,H})]^{\top}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(19)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">The final representation is formed by concatenation, <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\mathbf{v}^{(c)};\mathbf{v}^{(g)}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msup><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>;</mo><msup><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\mathbf{v}^{(c)};\mathbf{v}^{(g)}]</annotation></semantics></math>, which is then used for hallucination prediction, consistent with the formulation in the main text.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For entropy-based baselines, the feature function <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> computes the entropy of the attention distribution for each head:</p>
<table id="A3.E20" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E20.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="H(\mathbf{A}_{l,h})=-\sum_{i}a_{i}\log a_{i}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐀</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>log</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H(\mathbf{A}_{l,h})=-\sum_{i}a_{i}\log a_{i},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(20)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the normalized attention weight assigned to token <math id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Frequency-aware Operators</h3>

<section id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Discrete Fourier Transform.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For DFT, we separate low-frequency and high-frequency components using a frequency cutoff.
We systematically vary the cutoff threshold and evaluate hallucination detection performance across models, datasets, and sliding-window settings, as shown in <a href="#A4.F1" title="Figure A1 ‣ D.2 Full Results of Span-level Detection ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure A1</span></a>.
Across most settings, performance improves as the cutoff increases from low values, remains stable over a broad intermediate range, and drops sharply when the cutoff approaches the Nyquist limit.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Here, a normalized frequency of <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the Nyquist limit under the DFT formulation.
As shown in <a href="#A4.F1" title="Figure A1 ‣ D.2 Full Results of Span-level Detection ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure A1</span></a>, performance remains stable across a broad range of cutoff frequencies, but begins to degrade when the cutoff exceeds approximately 0.45, with a pronounced drop on the Nyquist boundary. This trend suggests that high-frequency attention variations relevant to hallucination detection are effectively captured below this transition point.
Empirically, we find that a cutoff frequency of 0.45 yields consistently strong and stable performance across models and datasets. Additionally, performance is relatively insensitive to lower cutoff settings, with improvements increasing gradually rather than abruptly—indicating robustness to the exact choice of cutoff within a reasonable range.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Discrete Wavelet Transform.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For DWT, we perform a multi-resolution decomposition of each attention signal <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{l,h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{l,h}</annotation></semantics></math> using the Daubechies-4 (db4) wavelet.
The db4 wavelet offers a favorable trade-off between locality and smoothness due to its vanishing moments, making it suitable for capturing abrupt transitions in attention distributions.
For boundary handling in finite-length attention sequences, we use zero padding for token-level detection and symmetric padding for span-level detection, based on overall performance observed across datasets and models.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We further compare depth-1 (level1) and depth-2 (level2) wavelet decompositions, as shown in <a href="#A4.T4" title="Table A4 ‣ D.2 Full Results of Span-level Detection ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table A4</span></a> and <a href="#A4.T5" title="Table A5 ‣ D.2 Full Results of Span-level Detection ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table A5</span></a>.
Empirically, a depth-1 decomposition consistently outperforms deeper decompositions across datasets and models.
We attribute this behavior to the fact that higher-level decompositions increasingly mix lower-frequency components into the detail coefficients, reducing their sensitivity to the finest-scale variations that are most informative for hallucination detection.
Accordingly, we adopt a level1 wavelet decomposition in all experiments.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Discrete Laplacian Operator.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The discrete Laplacian requires no cutoff or scale selection.
Instead, it directly computes second-order differences in the token domain, acting as a local high-pass filter that amplifies rapid attention fluctuations.
This simplicity makes the Laplacian operator computationally efficient and parameter-free, while still capturing localized high-frequency variation in attention distributions.
As discussed in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Discrete Laplacian Operator ‣ Appendix B Frequency-aware Operators’ Energy Equivalence ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>, the <math id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm of the Laplacian response corresponds to the discrete Dirichlet energy, providing a principled measure of attention roughness without additional hyperparameters.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.3 </span>Model Details</h3>

<section id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Inference.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A100 (80GB) GPUs.
The LLMs are kept frozen throughout.
We perform inference using teacher-forcing decoding with model response tokens to extract attention distributions for spectral analysis.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Classifiers.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our method uses a lightweight single-layer Logistic Regression classifier. This choice ensures that the detector does not introduce additional non-linear modeling capacity, and that performance differences primarily reflect the discriminative power of the proposed spectral features, rather than classifier expressiveness.
The linear detector was implemented using the <span id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scikit-learn</span> library. All hyperparameters, including the <math id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> penalty, were kept at their default values, with the exception of the maximum number of iterations, which was set to 1,000 to ensure model convergence.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For threshold-dependent metrics such as F1, the decision threshold is selected on a held-out validation split and fixed for test evaluation. In cases where an official validation set is not predefined, we reserve 10% of the original training data for this purpose.
We use AUROC as our primary metric because AUROC is threshold-independent and are unaffected by this choice.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.4 </span>Dataset Details</h3>

<div id="A3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use two publicly available contextual hallucination detection datasets in this work: RAGTruth and HalluRAG.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T1" class="ltx_table">

</table>
</figure>
<section id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">RAGTruth</h5>

<div id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">RAGTruth is a large-scale corpus designed for word-level hallucination detection within retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frameworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. It consists of 2,965 manually annotated responses with precise hallucination span labels across three primary tasks: question answering (QA), data-to-text (D2T), and summarization (Summ). The dataset provides standardized train and test splits for each task. Specifically, the QA, D2T, and Summ tasks comprise 839, 883, and 793 training samples, respectively, with each task sharing a consistent test set size of 150 samples.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">HalluRAG.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">HalluRAG focuses on sentence-level hallucination detection in RAG-based QA scenarios <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ridder and Schilling, 2024</a>)</cite>. It provides generated responses paired with sentence-level annotations, comprising 756 training, 162 validation, and 162 test samples.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">More details can be seen in <a href="#A3.T1" title="Table A1 ‣ C.4 Dataset Details ‣ Appendix C Experiment Details ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table A1</span></a>.
All token-level statistics are computed using the tokenizer corresponding to each model, and the reported values are averaged across models.
In particular, the hallucination ratio is defined as the number of hallucinated tokens in the response divided by the total number of response tokens. Since this ratio may vary across models, we report the average value over different models.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Additional Analysis and Results</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section reports the full experimental results and ablation studies omitted from the main text due to space constraints.
These results complement the analyses in the main paper and provide additional details on span-level detection, operator configurations, and the robustness of frequency-aware features across different settings.</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>Cross-domain Transfer Analysis</h3>

<div id="A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To examine whether the detector captures intrinsic attention-based signals rather than overfits task-specific artifacts, we conduct cross-domain transfer evaluation, where detectors are trained on one task domain and evaluated on another, as shown in <a href="#A4.T2" title="Table A2 ‣ D.1 Cross-domain Transfer Analysis ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table A2</span></a>. This experiment also serves to evaluate the generalization ability of the classifier and to test its susceptibility to overfitting.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table A2: </span>
Cross-domain evaluation. Models are trained on the column domain (Source) and evaluated on the row domain (Target). <span id="A4.T2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bold</span> values indicate in-domain performance (diagonal, Target=Source). Darker shading corresponds to higher cross-domain performance.</figcaption>

<td id="A4.T2.8.14.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.7pt 4.0pt;"><span id="A4.T2.8.14.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">0.7641</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, spectral-based detectors exhibit more stable cross-domain behavior compared to Lookback-Lens.
In particular, Fourier- and Wavelet-based variants maintain stronger performance when transferring across task boundaries, whereas Lookback-Lens shows larger performance degradation under domain shift.
This suggests that frequency-domain attention features capture more task-robust signals than heuristics based on attention mass or recency.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We also observe an asymmetric transfer pattern across tasks.
Models trained on QA generally transfer worse to Data-to-Text and Summarization than models trained on Data-to-Text or Summarization transferring to QA.
This asymmetry holds consistently across methods and detection granularities.
A plausible explanation is that QA exhibits more constrained and localized attention patterns, which may limit the generality of learned aggregation weights when applied to structurally different generation tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.3 </span>Full Results of Ablation Study</h3>

<div id="A4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section reports the full results corresponding to the attention-based analyses discussed in the main paper, evaluated across all datasets and models studied.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A4.F2" title="Figure A2 ‣ D.3 Full Results of Ablation Study ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure A2</span></a>reports the full results comparing low-pass and high-pass Fourier attention features across all evaluated models, datasets, and both token-level and span-level settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A4.F3" title="Figure A3 ‣ D.3 Full Results of Ablation Study ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure A3</span></a>shows the complete layer-wise importance profiles of frequency-aware attention features across models, including both token-level and span-level detection.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A4.T6" title="Table A6 ‣ D.3 Full Results of Ablation Study ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table A6</span></a>presents the full results of the head-level sparsity analysis, reporting detection performance when restricting attention features to the Top-<math id="A4.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> most important heads across datasets and models.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A4.T7" title="Table A7 ‣ D.3 Full Results of Ablation Study ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table A7</span></a>provides the complete ablation results comparing context-only and generated-only attention features for different spectral operators across all evaluation settings.</p>
</div>

<section id="A4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.4 </span>Examples of Raw Attention Signals</h3>

<div id="A4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A4.F4" title="Figure A4 ‣ D.4 Examples of Raw Attention Signals ‣ Appendix D Additional Analysis and Results ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure A4</span></a>presents qualitative examples of raw attention distributions from individual attention heads.
Each row corresponds to the same attention head at a fixed layer, while the left and right columns show attention over a hallucinated token and a non-hallucinated token, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We emphasize that these attention distributions reflect real model behavior and are substantially more irregular than the schematic examples shown in <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Modelswith Frequency-Aware Attention" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 2</span></a>.
In practice, attention weights are often sparse, unevenly distributed, and exhibit non-trivial fluctuations across token positions, rather than forming unimodal patterns <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nawrot et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Notably, for the examples shown in the top row, the two tokens share identical lookback ratios as measured by Lookback-Lens.
Similarly, for the bottom row, the context entropy of the two attention distributions is equal.
In these cases, these aggregate statistics alone are insufficient to distinguish hallucinated from non-hallucinated cases by visual inspection.
In contrast, after applying a high-pass filter to the same attention signals, the resulting high-frequency energy differs substantially between the two cases.
Although the raw attention curves may appear similar at a coarse level, frequency-domain filtering reveals differences in fine-grained variation patterns.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F4" class="ltx_figure">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A4.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure A4</span>: </span><span id="A4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Raw attention signal visualizations.
Each subfigure compares raw attention distributions for a hallucinated token (left) and a non-hallucinated token (right).
Red and yellow curves denote attention over context and generated tokens, respectively, when generating a hallucinated token,
while blue and green curves denote attention over context and generated tokens for a non-hallucinated token.
</span></figcaption>

    <a href="https://math.nist.gov/~BMiller/LaTeXML/" target="_blank" class="ltx_ref ltx_LaTeXML_logo">
      <span style="letter-spacing: -0.2em; margin-right: 0.1em;">
        L
        <span style="font-size: 70%; position: relative; bottom: 2.2pt;">A</span>
        T
        <span style="position: relative; bottom: -0.4ex;">E</span>
      </span>
      <span class="ltx_font_smallcaps">xml</span>
      <img alt="[LOGO]"
        src="data:image/png;base64,">
    </a>.
  </div>
  <div class="keyboard-glossary">
    <h2>Instructions for reporting errors</h2>
    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">
            <path
              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
  </div>
